title: Declarative Skills for AI Agents in Knowledge-Grounded Tool-Use Workflows
abstract: arXiv:2606.06923v2 Announce Type: replace  Abstract: We study how orchestration affects tool-using large language model (LLM) agents in customer-service workflows over an unstructured knowledge base, comparing a declarative agent that reads natural-language skill files, an imperative agent built on a state machine, and an unscaffolded baseline. The three are formalized as policy classes within one decentralized partially observable Markov decision process and evaluated on a complete design of five models, two retrieval regimes, and three agents, with paired tests. Averaged over all conditions, orchestration does not improve task success. The effect, however, depends on the quality of the agent's observation channel. Under perfect retrieval, skill files are neutral-to-negative on four of the five models; under embedding retrieval they are neutral-to-positive on four of the five. On the tasks where baseline and scaffold disagree, the declarative win rate rises from 42.4% to 62.7% (p = 0.

tldr: 该论文发现编排对工具使用型LLM智能体的作用取决于检索质量：完美检索时声明式技能文件中性甚至有害，嵌入检索时则有益，在基线与脚手架分歧的任务上声明式胜率从42.4%提升至62.7%。
en_tdlr: The effect of orchestration on tool-using LLM agents depends on retrieval quality: declarative skill files are neutral-to-negative under perfect retrieval but neutral-to-positive under embedding retrieval, with declarative win rates rising from 42.4% to 62.7% on tasks where baseline and scaffold disagree.
